title: Designing a stock exchange

facts.text: The aim is microsecond latency, reached by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage.

The trading flow is the critical path with strict latency requirements: an order enters the order manager, passes mandatory risk checks, is matched, and the execution leaves through the order manager.
The market data flow and the reporting flow are not on the critical path and have different latency requirements, so non-critical tasks are removed from the trading flow.

Clients send orders, instructions to buy or sell, to a broker or directly to the exchange; FIX, the standard protocol for pre-trade communications and trade execution, carries them as numeric tag and value fields.

FIX sessions use sequence numbers and retransmission on request, so delivery survives a disconnection; high-performance sessions can instead pick idempotent or unsequenced delivery, since retransmission delays are often undesirable in fast markets.
Binary encodings such as Simple Binary Encoding cut latency, because no translation is needed to put data into a format computers can use, and fixed-length fields make performance more deterministic.
A market order executes at once at the best available price, giving certainty of execution but no price control; a limit order executes only at its limit price or better and may never fill.

Time-in-force and conditional instructions add rules: day orders expire at the session close, good-til-cancelled orders persist, immediate-or-cancel allows partial fills, and a stop order activates at its stop price.

The order book is the data model: a list of buy orders and a list of sell orders, each entry holding the party, the number of securities and the price, with orders at one price grouped into a price level.
The top of the book is the highest bid and lowest ask; their gap is the bid-ask spread, and book depth is the number of price levels kept.
The matching engine uses the book to decide which orders can be fully or partially executed; a bid at or above the lowest ask fills at once, and a partly filled limit order rests on the book.
Matching priority favors market orders, then limit orders first-come-first-served, with conditional orders ranked by when their condition is met and iceberg or dark-pool orders lower.

Market data, the latest bid, ask and last trade, is published off the critical path; delivery is highly time-sensitive, ticker plants handle the streams, and UDP multicast serves many recipients at once.
All components run on a single giant server with no containers, and shared memory serves as the event bus with no hard disk; other components listen on the bus and react.
The order manager and matching engine are single-threaded on the critical path and each is pinned to a CPU, so there is no context switch and no locks; the loop runs tasks one by one in sequence.

Locks block threads and risk deadlock and priority inversion, so a design avoids them in shared structures: lock-free data structures raise parallel performance, and a single-reader single-writer ring buffer needs only a memory barrier.

notes: thin: the crawled sources give no order or trade volumes, estimates, exchange-specific API, or failover and recovery of the single-server design; the 14 steps of the trading flow, sequencer and pre-trade risk checks are not described in text.

title: Low-latency critical path design

definition.text: Getting very low latency by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage.

facts.text: A modern stock exchange reaches microsecond latency with the principle of doing less on the critical path.

Tasks that are not critical should be removed from the critical path; for example the market data flow and the reporting flow are off the exchange's critical path and have different latency requirements.
Key components on the critical path can be single-threaded, each pinned to a CPU, so there is no context switch and no locks, and run one task after another in a single loop.
Components can talk through shared memory used as an event bus instead of a hard disk, and be deployed together on one giant server without containers.

notes: General principle drawn from the exchange guides; the exchange itself is in the Worked example.

definition.text: The list of orders that a trading venue, in particular a stock exchange, uses to record the interest of buyers and sellers in a financial instrument.

facts.text: A securities order book holds a list of buy orders and a list of sell orders.
Each entry keeps the number of securities, the price the buyer or seller bids or asks, and some means of identifying the party, even if that identity is obscured as in a dark pool.
Orders at the same price sit on one price level; a bid arriving at that price could potentially be filled by any of the sell orders on that level.
A matching engine uses the book to decide which orders can be fully or partially executed; a bid equal to or higher than the lowest ask is filled at once and never joins the open book.
If such crossing orders stay unmatched because of an error or a market condition, the book is said to be crossed.
The highest bid and the lowest ask are the top of the book; they signal the prevailing market, and the difference between them is the bid-ask spread.
Book depth is the number of price levels in the book; a book can be kept to a fixed depth, with orders beyond it ignored or rejected, or hold unlimited levels.

definition.text: The standard instructions a trader can place on a trading venue, such as market, limit and stop orders, each with its own execution rules.

facts.text: A market order executes immediately at the best available price and is filled as long as willing counterparties exist; it gives certainty of execution but no control over the price received.
In fast-moving markets a market order's fill price can differ widely from the last quote, and the order may be split across several counterparties at different prices.
A buy limit order executes only at the limit price or lower and a sell limit order only at the limit price or higher; the trader controls the price but the order may never be filled.
A limit order that the book can satisfy on arrival is marketable; it may be filled in part from the book, with the rest added to the book.

Fill-or-kill orders are filled completely on the first attempt or cancelled, all-or-none orders must be filled in full or not at all, and immediate-or-cancel orders execute at once but allow partial fills.
A day order lasts until the end of the day's trading session; a good-til-cancelled order persists until a cancelling order, although brokers may set limits such as 90 days.
A conditional order executes only when a condition is met: a stop order becomes active when the price reaches the stop price, and a stop-limit order then becomes a limit order.

title: Matching engine

definition.text: The component that uses the order book to determine which buy and sell orders can be fully or partially executed.

facts.text: A matching engine uses the order book to determine which orders can be fully or partially executed; orders are matched as the interest of buyers and sellers can be satisfied.
An order whose bid is equal to or higher than the lowest ask can be fulfilled immediately and does not become part of the open orders book.
A limit order may be partially filled from the book with the remainder added to the book, and a market order may be split across several counterparties at different prices.

Electronic markets give market orders the highest priority, then limit orders first-come-first-served; conditional orders get priority by the time their condition is met, and iceberg and dark-pool orders get lower priority.
In a low-latency exchange design the matching engine is single-threaded on the critical path and pinned to a CPU, so there is no context switch and no locks.

notes: thin: no crawled page on order matching systems; matching algorithms such as price-time or pro-rata priority, and how the engine handles auctions, are not described.

definition.text: Price and other related data for a financial instrument, reported by a trading venue such as a stock exchange.

facts.text: A market data record carries the instrument identifier (ticker symbol and exchange code), the latest bid and ask price and the time of the last trade, and may add volume traded and bid and offer sizes.
Quote data (bid, ask and their sizes) and trade data (last sale, last size, volume) are often generated over different data feeds.
Delivering prices from exchanges to users is highly time-sensitive, so specialized ticker plants collect and push massive data streams fast enough to feed trading systems before markets change.

Distribution platforms compress or represent data with specially designed protocols to raise throughput or reduce latency; UDP multicast delivers it efficiently to many recipients at once, and the FAST binary protocol exists for multicast market data.

In a feed handler, sources connect to a server that redistributes data: it forwards a client's subscription to the sources if it has no cached data, then sends every update for an instrument to all subscribed clients.
A feed handler server applies two permission levels: login permission to connect, and information permission to view an instrument.

Market data is either real-time or delayed price quotations; static reference data, such as identifier codes and security terms, does not change in real time and usually originates from the issuer, while prices originate from the exchanges.

definition.text: An electronic communications protocol for the real-time exchange of information about securities transactions and markets.

facts.text: FIX is the standard electronic protocol for pre-trade communications and trade execution, used by the buy side and sell side, including mutual funds, investment banks, brokers, stock exchanges and ECNs.
Classic FIX tagvalue messages are ASCII text: each field is a numeric tag plus a value separated by the SOH character, so messages are self-describing; a message has a header, a body and a trailer.
Body length counts characters from tag 35 up to tag 10, and the checksum is the last field, tag 10: the sum of the ASCII values of all other characters modulo 256, written as three characters.
The FIXT session layer is a point-to-point protocol usually run over TCP, and it guarantees message delivery in both directions.

Messages in each direction carry a sequence number; after a communication fault a peer may request retransmission of missed messages, and delivery survives disconnection and a later reestablished session.

Simple Binary Encoding uses native binary types in fixed positions, giving much lower latency and more deterministic performance than character-based tagvalue, whose variable-length fields were judged no longer fit for high performance trading.

The FIXP session layer for high performance trading lets peers negotiate delivery guarantees: recoverable (exactly-once, with retransmission), idempotent (at-most-once) or unsequenced; delays from retransmission are often undesirable in fast markets.
FAST is a binary protocol used mostly for sending multicast market data over UDP connections.

definition.text: Also called CPU pinning, it binds a process or thread to a CPU or a range of CPUs so that it executes only on the designated processors.

facts.text: A thread that resumes on the CPU it ran on before may find data still in that CPU's cache and take fewer cache misses, but pinning forces it to wait for that CPU to become free.
Pinning suits CPU-intensive processes with few interrupts; an ordinary program, which is interrupted more often and ends up waiting more, might instead be slowed down.
On NUMA systems the latency comes from L3 misses and cross-node memory access, so constraining all threads of a program to one NUMA node lets them share an L3 cache.
Affinity statically divides processing resources, which leaves cores unused when no other program runs; on Linux it is set with the taskset program or the sched_setaffinity system call.

definition.text: An algorithm is non-blocking if the failure or suspension of any thread cannot cause the failure or suspension of another thread.

facts.text: A non-blocking algorithm is lock-free if there is guaranteed system-wide progress and wait-free if there is also guaranteed per-thread progress; obstruction-freedom is the weakest guarantee, and every lock-free algorithm is obstruction-free.

Locks block threads that cannot accomplish anything while waiting, can cause deadlock, livelock and priority inversion, and force a trade-off between coarse-grained locking, which limits parallelism, and error-prone fine-grained locking.

A lock-free data structure spends more time in parallel rather than serial execution, improving performance on a multi-core processor because access to shared data need not be serialized; it is also safe in interrupt handlers.
Non-blocking algorithms use atomic read-modify-write primitives provided by the hardware, most notably compare-and-swap, in a carefully designed order of reads, read-modify-writes and writes.
Compilers and many CPUs reorder operations unless told not to, so memory barriers are needed; C++11 std::atomic and C11 stdatomic.h supply types that stop the compiler reordering and insert barriers.
A single-reader single-writer ring buffer FIFO can be implemented safely with only a memory barrier, since some non-blocking structures are weak enough to need no special atomic primitives.

It is difficult to write lock-free code that is correct; wait-free designs from universal constructions perform below blocking designs, and without hard deadlines wait-free algorithms may not be worth their extra complexity.
